debate.situation: The user introduced three new skincare products simultaneously and is experiencing facial stinging, leaving them unable to identify the specific product causing the reaction. The core tension lies between the need for immediate relief and the desire to isolate the irritant for future prevention.

debate.speaker: The Empiricist
debate.text: You have created a muddle of variables. To find the truth, you must stop all three immediately. As it is written, The true method of experience first lights the candle, and then by means of the candle shows the way.
debate.author: Francis Bacon

debate.speaker: The Minimalist
debate.text: I agree that stopping is necessary, but the error was starting three at once. You should focus on the essential task of healing your skin, which means stripping away everything that is not absolutely required.
debate.author: Greg McKeown

debate.speaker: The Pragmatist
debate.text: The goal is comfort. If it stings, the only thing that matters is stopping the pain. We do not need a laboratory; we need a solution that works to restore your skin to its normal state.
debate.author: William James

debate.speaker: The Empiricist
debate.text: But if you do not identify the culprit, you will repeat the error. We must reintroduce them one by one, allowing enough time for the skin to react to each specific substance.
debate.author: Francis Bacon

debate.speaker: The Minimalist
debate.text: Reintroducing them is just adding noise back into a system that is already failing. Perhaps none of them are essential, and you should consider if your skin is better off without these additions entirely.
debate.author: Greg McKeown

debate.speaker: The Pragmatist
debate.text: I previously thought comfort was the only metric, but the Empiricist is right. If I want to keep using products, I need to know which one is the problem. My position has shifted; we must test them to gain the knowledge required to avoid future pain.
debate.author: William James

debate.speaker: The Empiricist
debate.text: Precisely. By isolating one variable at a time, we move from mere opinion to a verified fact about which product your skin rejects.
debate.author: Francis Bacon

debate.speaker: The Minimalist
debate.text: If you must test, keep it essential. Do not test all three. Pick the one you suspect most and observe. Do not over-complicate the recovery process with a rigid, lengthy schedule.
debate.author: Greg McKeown

debate.speaker: The Pragmatist
debate.text: That is a useful compromise. We test the most likely offender first. If that one is fine, we move to the next. The truth of the matter is what works to identify the irritant with the least amount of suffering.
debate.author: William James

debate.clearer: The debate clarified that while immediate cessation is the only way to stop the stinging, a systematic reintroduction is necessary to avoid future reactions. The main dispute remains whether to test all products or only the most suspicious ones, as the Minimalist warns against unnecessary complexity while the Empiricist insists on thoroughness.
debate.dependsOn: If the stinging is severe, stop all products immediately until the skin fully recovers, as testing on inflamed skin is unreliable. If you suspect one product specifically (e.g., a new active ingredient), test that one first after recovery. If the irritation persists even after stopping all three, the issue may be a reaction to the combination or an unrelated environmental factor, in which case consulting a dermatologist is the most proportionate next step.
